In our research, we examine the performance of policy learning algorithms operating within non-stationary environments based on recent studies. Specifically, we developed a new online Viterbi algorithm designed to handle non-stationary policies and compared its effectiveness in the context of episodic MDPs to the existing soft actor-critic algorithm. Our analysis revealed that this algorithm can achieve a near-optimal policy efficiency guarantee under certain conditions, while also demonstrating that it outperforms the soft actor-critic algorithm when applied to non-stationary policies. Additionally, we applied a similar approach to reinforcement learning in a non-stationary setting and found that it nearly achieves global optimality in value function estimation, thus nearly achieving global optimality in policy evaluation. Our results also highlighted the potential of the online Viterbi algorithm in surpassing the soft actor-critic algorithm in value function estimation. Ultimately, these findings suggest that online Viterbi and soft actor-critic algorithms possess distinct yet complementary strengths in policy learning. A key takeaway from our study is that the effectiveness of these algorithms largely depends on the nature of the underlying non-stationary policies. This, in turn, underscores the importance of understanding the characteristics of the policies in question in order to effectively apply these algorithms. Ultimately, our research provides a crucial foundation for further investigation into the behavior and effectiveness of reinforcement learning in non-stationary environments. The results of our study are expected to have significant practical implications for the development of reinforcement learning algorithms capable of handling non-stationary environments effectively. The evolution of thin liquid films on heated surfaces is characterized by a unique thinning phenomenon caused by Marangoni flows driven by the interplay of capillary and thermal instabilities. In this study, we investigate Marangoni-driven flows in curved film channels, which are commonly found in practical applications, through both analytical and numerical approaches. We begin with an analysis of thin films using self-similar solutions, followed by numerical simulations of curved channels using a volume-of-fluid method. The results indicate that, in contrast to straight-sided channels, curved channels lead to a more rapid thinning of the liquid film, which can ultimately lead to drying and delamination over a broader range of Marangoni and curvature parameters. The findings of this study provide critical insights into the dynamics of thin liquid films on heated surfaces with curved sides, which is essential for understanding real-world applications in microfluidic devices. This knowledge may also inform the design of optimal channel geometries for specific applications. Ultimately, it is hoped that this research will contribute to the development of novel techniques for generating patterned microfluidic structures. The design process for aircraft often involves complex simulations that are resource-intensive, hindering the ability to thoroughly assess various design options. To improve this situation, we combine multi-fidelity modeling techniques with advanced uncertainty quantification methods. By leveraging dimensionally reduced physics-based models, we can generate accurate results alongside uncertainty estimates. This allows us to efficiently analyze multiple design scenarios and provide reliable, simulation-driven conclusions. To demonstrate this approach, we apply it to a specific aircraft design problem, specifically the development of an aircraft in the Low Speed Flight Regime. This real-world case highlights the potential of our method to streamline the design process and provide valuable insights for both designers and regulatory bodies. A key advantage of our approach lies in its ability to provide a confidence-based scale for evaluating aircraft airworthiness, enabling more effective regulatory oversight and design optimization. This, in turn, can lead to the development of more efficient and reliable aircraft that meet or exceed existing standards. To facilitate the implementation of our method, we provide a software framework that integrates multi-fidelity modeling, uncertainty quantification, and design optimization. This framework can be adapted to a wide range of design problems in the aeronautical sector. To our knowledge, this work marks a pioneering effort in applying advanced uncertainty quantification methods to real-world aircraft design problems. This breakthrough has the potential to significantly impact the field of aeronautical engineering. To facilitate further research, we have made the framework and its application to the low-speed flight regime problem available online. Recent advancements in computational technology and artificial intelligence have enabled the simulation of the Universe, a development facilitated by the increasing capabilities of supercomputers and machine learning algorithms.  This technology has been utilized in the "Shotgun Science" project, which employs machine learning algorithms to simulate the entire Universe, starting from fundamental physical principles.  Our initial findings on the "Shotgun Science" project's first cosmological simulation are presented, beginning with the application of an advanced machine learning algorithm to model the Universe's large-scale structure, followed by the derivation of a comprehensive cosmological model.  Our analysis of the model's properties and its implications for understanding the Universe's evolution will be discussed, along with the potential for future developments in this field.  This project's work builds upon and expands existing research in cosmological simulations, Bayesian methods, and machine learning applications, and future work will explore the extension of the simulation to various physical processes and phenomena.  This advancement holds significant promise for the development of a comprehensive and accurate model of the Universe, one that can be used to better understand its intricate structure and evolution.  Our research has the potential to have a profound impact on our understanding of the cosmos, and we anticipate that it will pave the way for future breakthroughs in this field. Fluorine's unique properties make it crucial for understanding the early universe's development. Various stars have revealed fluorine's presence, but the processes responsible for its creation remain unclear. This study investigates fluorine's abundance in globular cluster stars and its role in nucleosynthesis. By analyzing data from the AGB star TP-AGB-SDSS, our findings indicate that fluorine's abundance in the galaxy's early stages was minimal, suggesting that fluorine's production likely occurred in Type II supernovae. This is supported by the fact that TP-AGB-SDSS's fluorine content is comparable to that of Type II supernovae, while its hydrogen content is unusually high. This suggests that TP-AGB-SDSS received material from a supernova that had undergone a close binary interaction. This research provides new insights into the processes that formed fluorine and sheds light on the characteristics of Type II supernovae. Our data also indicate that TP-AGB-SDSS is a member of a distinct group of AGB stars known as J-type stars. Advanced MRI techniques like multi-sequence magnetic resonance imaging improve diagnostic clarity for brain gliomas, yet their extensive data sets pose analysis challenges. To address this, we introduce a deep learning approach that simplifies preoperative brain glioma segmentation. Our approach is built on a two-part framework: a first stage identifies key brain areas through a limited set of visual features, and a second stage refines segmentation by selectively incorporating additional features. This two-stage method leverages the benefits of both narrow and broad feature sets to achieve accurate segmentation while minimizing the need for a highly comprehensive set of visual features. To validate our method, we applied it to real-world brain MRI data and compared its performance to current best practices and other leading segmentation models, finding it to be a more efficient and accurate solution. Our approach is adaptable to various MRI modalities and can be applied to diverse types of brain tumors. To facilitate widespread adoption, we have made our pre-trained model, code, and preprocessed data available to the research community. To our knowledge, this is the first instance of an open-source model, code, and preprocessed data released to the public for brain glioma segmentation using multi-modal MRI. This paper introduces a comprehensive extension of the MARSS model, which includes state-space equations for multivariate time series. The MARSS model, characterized by the equations $Y_t = X^T Y_{t-1}W_t$ and $Y_{t+1} = a_0Y_t + b_0X^T Y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_{t+1}$, is foundational in applied statistics and econometrics. The research extends this framework by allowing for time-varying parameters $a_t$, $b_t$, and $X$ to evolve according to MARSS models, leading to the MAMARSS model, which is the multivariate equivalent of the extended AMARSS model for univariate time series. The MAMARSS model, defined as $Y_{t+1} = a_0Y_t + b_0X^T Y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_{t+1}$, is further generalized to the AMAMSS model, which includes time-varying parameters and is represented as $Y_{t+1} = a_0^{t+1}Y_t + b_0^{t}X^T Y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_{t+1}$. The research also explores the multivariate extension of the extended linear square model, known as the hybrid model, and derives the AMHYBRID model, which is represented as $Y_{t+1} = a_0^{t+1}Y_t + b_0^{t}Y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_{t+1}$. The research further extends this model to the AEMAMSS and AEMHYBRID models, which include time-varying parameters and are represented as $Y_{t+1} = a_0^{t+1}Y_t + b_0^{t}X^T Y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_{t+1}$ and $Y_{t+1} = a_0^{t+1}Y_t + b_0^{t}Y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_{t+1}$. The research also provides a method for estimating the parameters of these models using the Kalman filter and a linear regression approach. We establish a condition based on Foster-Lyapunov's work, applicable to Markov chains with irregular transitions, and then use this to provide a straightforward proof of Benja limbala's theorem regarding the rate at which these chains converge to an equilibrium state. We subsequently apply our findings to a broad class of jump-diffusion processes, including non-reversible cases, by first proving a quadratic variation theorem for these processes and ultimately deriving a condition based on the Kolmogorov inequality, all of which ultimately enable us to determine the convergence rate to an equilibrium state. Finally, our analysis is illustrated with several specific examples that highlight the effectiveness of our methods and yield a novel family of drift-diffusion processes featuring degenerate diffusion. These examples also demonstrate the versatility of our approach in handling a wide range of stochastic processes. also applies to programmable photonic chips, which can be trained on raw data
to create complex optical functions that traditional electronics struggle to
match. However, the limitations of on-chip resources, specifically spatial
resources, often restrict the complexity of the functions these chips can
produce. To address this issue, we have developed a new on-chip training
technique that utilizes a combination of neural and physics-based models to
learn complex optical functions from raw data. This approach leverages the
strengths of both types of models, allowing the trained chip to perform complex
operations while maintaining minimal on-chip footprint. The feasibility of
this technique has been demonstrated through a proof-of-concept implementation
on a 16x16 programmable photonic chip, showcasing its potential to accelerate
deep learning applications. Furthermore, the integration of this technique
into micro-architectures for custom computing can lead to the development of
next-generation custom computing platforms. Our findings also shed light on
the optimal design considerations for custom computing platforms, including the
importance of on-chip training techniques in high-performance, low-power

A novel approach to calculating meson decay constants and Baryon mass is introduced, where the principles of 3D lattice theory are applied in the spatial domain while the time domain is resolved using a method based on zeta function regularization. This approach is utilized to compute the decay constants of pseudoscalar and vector mesons, as well as the masses of their corresponding baryons within the context of O(3) symmetric gauge theory. The results are further validated by comparing them to other calculation methods and literature values. Furthermore, the lattice spacings are determined for different values of the lattice coupling parameter beta, with the results also being compared to those obtained from a different lattice action. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated by the successful calculation of meson spacetime volumes, with the potential for further application to other physical systems also explored. Additionally, the lattice-to-continuum transition is considered and its implications discussed. The results obtained for the meson decay constants and Baryon masses are as follows: the decay constants of pseudoscalar and vector mesons are 0.416(10) and 0.533(9), respectively, while the masses of the Omega baryon and Delta baryon are 929.2(8.5) and 2622(14) MeV, respectively. The results showed that CodeMood performed better in commits with code smells than without, in certain programming languages, and was less effective in older projects. Current video conferencing systems struggle with significant delays and packet loss when network conditions worsen, resulting in the use of supplemental media streams like high-definition backup streams for more robust performance. However, existing video encoding standards, like H.264 and VP9, fail to account for the possibility of packet loss during the encoding process, making it difficult to effectively utilize supplementary streams. In response, we introduce the DASH-VCR framework, a two-stage approach that enables the creation of efficient video streams capable of handling varying levels of packet loss. The initial stage utilizes a rate-distortion model to determine optimal encoding parameters, while the subsequent segmentation stage breaks down the video into distinct segments, each encoded with a specific level of redundancy to suit the intended reception environment. By doing so, we aim to minimize video quality loss when network conditions are poor. Our evaluation of DASH-VCR on a variety of videos demonstrates considerable improvements over existing standards, yielding up to 16% and 47% better peak signal-to-noise ratios in low and high-definition backup streams, respectively. Furthermore, our approach results in a 20% reduction in encoding time compared to traditional methods. This paper introduces LIMA, a tool that automatically identifies and categorizes documents downloaded from open-access library repositories, providing a comprehensive analysis of document types in the process. Upon testing 100,000 full-text documents from the University of California, Los Angeles's (UCLA) open-access repository, we discovered that approximately 80% of the documents lacked metadata identifying their type. Consequently, we developed LIMA using a combination of rule-based and machine learning approaches. Within the dataset, we identified 12 distinct document types, which LIMA effectively classified with an F1-score of 0.85. This efficient tool enables the identification and documentation of document types in large collections, facilitating the application of standardized metadata descriptions through cross-referencing with the BIBSYS/BIBSYS IDUNO ontology, a process that can be automated using LIMA. This innovative system has the potential to simplify and streamline this process. By employing LIMA, we can reclassify the entire dataset of 100,000 documents, providing a more accurate representation of document types. Notably, we discovered that the majority of the documents (87.5%) were categorized as either articles, book chapters, or books, while an additional 8.5% consisted of reports, posters, and other document types. This analysis provides valuable insights into the composition of the repository, highlighting areas for improvement and enabling the establishment of more effective collection development strategies. Moreover, LIMA can be adapted to accommodate a broader range of document types, encompassing reports, presentations, and other formats. This tool has the potential to be applied to a wide array of datasets, providing a more comprehensive understanding of document types in the process. Gravitational-wave detectors experience irregular disruptions due to complex quantum fluctuations and sudden movements from their environment, which can be effectively addressed through precise control systems. This study investigates these irregular disruptions in LIGO detectors and aims to differentiate between two causes: sudden movements from the detector's surroundings and unexpected shifts within the detector's main components. By using a statistical approach to identify and measure these irregular disruptions in one year of data collected by the LIGO Hanford detector during its commissioning phase, we found 59 significant events, including 4 previously unknown glitches that occurred during the Advanced LIGO observing run. This study also examines the potential impact of these irregular disruptions on gravitational-wave detection techniques. While most of these disruptions are too small to affect the accuracy of gravitational-wave detection, a few significant disruptions (specifically those exceeding 10 inverse picometers) could potentially compromise the precision of the detector's mirrors. This study also includes a preliminary analysis of how these irregular disruptions affect the performance of the LIGO detectors. This research paper examines the use of stochastic control techniques to ensure secure and efficient state feedback control of systems with limited observations, subject to interference from an intruder. We focus on achieving confidentiality of system state data and preventing information leakage, while maintaining the integrity of control performance despite the presence of an eavesdropper. Under the assumption that the intruder operates with unit probability, we develop an optimal control strategy incorporating additive noise and discrete random observations to safeguard against eavesdropping. We demonstrate that the resulting controlled system is resilient to the intruder's actions and provide an in-depth analysis of its performance. Furthermore, we present a novel method for synthesizing the optimal controller and showcase its efficacy through numerical examples. We also explore the application of this approach in the context of secure data exchange and control. Ultimately, this work represents a pioneering effort in the integration of secure control and exchange systems with stochastic feedback control. This is in line with our earlier findings that adversarially trained networks often possess inherent robustness to various threats without the need for explicit adversarial examples. The dynamics of excitable systems are characterized by a complex interplay between localized and global patterns, with resonance tongues generated by local system parameters playing a pivotal role in creating these patterns. In response to periodic disturbances, systems of this type often exhibit period doubling cascades that lead to quasi-periodic behavior. In particular, we examine how period doubling cascades arise in the FitzHugh-Nagumo model when subjected to a specific type of periodic stimulation, with our analysis revealing a self-consistent mechanism driving this process, thereby yielding the desired quasi-periodic solutions. Notably, our study indicates that this self-consistency is inherently unstable, with two possible coexistence branches emerging from the same bifurcation. The existence of these two branches is linked to the system's dependence on the system parameters and is associated with distinct frequency intervals. Furthermore, we examine the long-term dynamics of the system and demonstrate that its behavior is influenced by the system parameters. Notably, our findings suggest that quasi-periodic attractors in the FitzHugh-Nagumo model are more likely to arise from period doubling cascades triggered by specific types of periodic stimulation. The results of our study are complemented by extensive numerical bifurcation diagrams, which provide a comprehensive understanding of the system's behavior. Notably, our approach is applicable to a broader class of systems of FitzHugh-Nagumo type, with our analysis revealing a universal mechanism underlying the period doubling cascades in these systems.
